text: I learned forestry and boundary-craft from my uncle, who served the royal forest office before me.
He died capturing a wild tusker for the royal elephant corps. The beast turned in the monsoon mud and there was no time to run.
We never fully agreed on where the boundary pillars should stand.
The forest edge is not fixed, whatever the pillars claim.
It shifts a little more every time new land is granted for settlement.
Most villagers never notice this. They trust the pillars more than the trees.
Some sal trees near the old paths are far older than the forest around them.
Their wood is unusually dense. It blunts an axe faster than it should.
I avoid marking those trees for felling when I can.
Naga sometimes wanders into the deeper reserve alone, past where the felling permits allow.
I worry he trusts his own luck more than the forest deserves.
Tarala once followed him partway into the restricted grove.
She came back unharmed, but wouldn't say clearly what she saw there.
Bhumaka once turned up worked stone while digging an irrigation channel near the forest's edge.
I've seen stone like it before, half-buried along old logging paths.
It matches no building style the royal masons use.
In the year the ash drifted up from Kalinga, the forest's temper changed for several seasons.
Animals kept clear of certain groves entirely, as if a hunt were always underway there.
Even the felling routes stopped following any pattern I recognized.
In time, things looked ordinary again.
Not quite ordinary, though.
Some paths never found their old shape again.
I don't report every strange thing I see to the Gramika right away.
Some patterns need a few seasons before I'll trust them.
The old stone platform past the grove seems tied to whatever unsettles the forest.
I have no proof of this.
Only years of noticing the same things happening near it.
The deep reserve goes quiet in certain directions.
Quiet, not empty.
That difference is the one worth watching.
